chunks: What bandwidth characterizes. The question: What does the bandwidth characterize?
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a circuit can pass without cutting them down much.
We usually measure it between the two points where the output is 3 decibels below its normal level (about 70. 7% of the voltage).
It tells you how quickly a system can respond, so it is also a limit on how fast a signal can change.
Think of a road with several lanes. A wider road carries more traffic at once. Likewise, a wider bandwidth carries more kinds of signals, and faster changes, through the circuit.
But a wide road also lets in more roadside noise, so you don't build it wider than you need.

A low Q means a wide, shallow band-pass; a narrow-band filter has a high Q .
Bandwidth: the width of the frequency range that passes, from the lower -3 decibels point to the upper one.
Passband: the range of frequencies the circuit passes at about full strength. -3 decibels point: where the output is 70. 7% of the passband level.
Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from 10% to 90% of its final value. Gain-bandwidth product: for an op-amp, gain times bandwidth stays about constant.
A system with bandwidth B has a rise time of about 0. 35 over B . A 100 megahertz oscilloscope therefore has a rise time of 0. 35 over (100 times 10 to the 6) equals 3.
5 nanoseconds. If you feed it a faster edge, you will still see an edge of about 3. 5 nanoseconds on the screen. That is the whole idea.
"Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a system passes within 3 decibels of its passband gain: DC to the corner for a low-pass, upper minus lower edge for a band-pass.
It characterizes speed: rise time is about 0. 35 over the bandwidth. It also sets how much noise gets in and, through Shannon, how much information you can send.
For an op-amp, closed-loop bandwidth is about GBW over gain."
